query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Bulk alloying the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with trace amounts of reactive elements (specifically, a combined ~0.5 atomic percent of Y and Hf) will enhance its high-temperature and room-temperature stability by stabilizing its fine lamellar microstructure and by promoting the formation of adherent, protective oxide films. This modification will improve its resistance to corrosion, reduce creep under long-term mechanical loading, and yield higher overall strength without sacrificing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniformly cast, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy composed of alternating FCC (L12) and B2 phases exhibiting mechanical properties below industrial fastener requirements.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor bulk addition of reactive elements (≈0.5 at.% total of Y and Hf) during alloy melting.
generation.conditions: The alloy is intended for use as fasteners subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations (from room temperature up to ≈700°C), long-term cyclic or sustained mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., molten salt or chloride-rich media).
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of Y and Hf at grain and phase boundaries in the lamellar microstructure, which reinforces the boundaries against coarsening during thermal cycling and facilitates the formation of an adherent, protective oxide film during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The reactive elements are expected to segregate to the eutectic lamella boundaries and phase interfaces, lowering boundary energies and retarding grain growth or phase coarsening during thermal fluctuations. In addition, Y and Hf are known to improve oxide scale adhesion, which minimizes spallation under hot corrosion conditions. These effects combine to limit room-temperature creep (through stabilized boundaries) and maintain balanced strength and ductility under long-term loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped alloy, the Y/Hf-modified alloy should show lower corrosion rates and reduced oxide scale spallation at high temperatures, improved resistance to room-temperature creep, and an increase in yield strength and endurance under long-term mechanical loading—all while retaining its advantageous dual-phase ductility.
generation.baseline: The original, as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy in its fine lamellar state, which, although exhibiting a good strength-ductility synergy, lacks sufficient resistance to extreme thermal fluctuations, long-term creep, and corrosive attack for use in demanding fastener applications.
generation.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective provided that the trace addition is kept low (≈0.5 at.%), so as not to alter the fundamental lamellar architecture or induce unwanted secondary phases. Its beneficial effects are expected within operating temperatures from ambient up to ≈700°C and in corrosive environments similar to those tested (such as molten salt or chloride-containing acid solutions). Exceeding these dopant concentrations or operating conditions outside this range may negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: While the positive effects of Y and Hf on hot corrosion resistance and thermal stability are documented in laser-clad coatings (PMC10488378) and the role of microstructural interfaces in strength is established (PMC6353877), uncertainty remains in translating these benefits to bulk alloy modifications. It is also not fully clear how these dopants will influence room-temperature creep behavior in the bulk alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of standard (undoped) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with a 0.5 at.% combined addition of Y and Hf. Process both via identical melting and heat-treatment schedules to achieve a uniform fine lamellar microstructure. Subject specimens to (a) accelerated hot corrosion tests in a molten salt environment (e.g., 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl at 900°C for 60 hours), (b) cyclic thermal exposure from room temperature to 700°C to assess microstructural stability, and (c) long-term creep tests at room temperature under constant load. Concurrently, perform standard tensile tests to extract yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
measurements: Corrosion rate (quantified by weight loss and percentage of spallation area)
Tensile properties (yield strength, UTS, and elongation)
Creep strain rate under sustained loading at room temperature
Post-test microstructural analysis (grain/lamella boundary stability via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., ≥15% reduction in corrosion rate and creep strain rate, along with maintained or improved tensile properties) compared to the baseline alloy under the specified test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
